note: Sydney's daily life (issue #357): the people to know, their hours, the jobs, the counters and the calendar. Built into web/data/sydney/life.json by pipeline/life.py, which resolves every place. Literal [x, y] places are copied from web/data/sydney/game.json (wharf terminals, trig stations, road vertices), never measured by hand.

bonds.title: The Opera House guide
bonds.busy: I've tours back to back till the light goes. Find me in the evening or after dark, when the houses are in and the forecourt's quiet.

ranks.title: Before the sails
ranks.invite: You keep looking up. Everyone does. Got a bit of the {slot}? I'll tell you what you'd have been looking at instead.
talk: Seventy years ago you'd be standing in a tram shed. Fort Macquarie depot, built with battlements like a toy castle. They knocked it down in 1958 to build this.
And before any of that it was Bennelong's point. The governor had a brick hut built for him here in 1790. It's still his name on the point.
ranks.fact: The Opera House stands on Bennelong Point, where the Fort Macquarie tram depot stood until it was demolished in 1958.

ask.q: When they started, how long did they say it would take to build?

options.reply: Four years and seven million dollars. It took fourteen, and a hundred and two million. Nobody's asked for the money back.
That's what it took: fourteen. The promise was four years and seven million dollars. The bill came to a hundred and two.

request.text: Climb to the trig station on the Opera House steps
request.ask: Been up the steps yet? There's a trig station at the top. Best seat on the harbour, and it's free.

ranks.title: Two hundred and thirty-three
talk: You went up. Then you'll have seen the tiles are two colours, not one: gloss white and matt cream, so the shells never glare.
Utzon was thirty-eight and had never set foot in Australia when he won. Two hundred and thirty-three entries from thirty-two countries, and the Dane who'd studied the harbour off sea charts got it.
ranks.fact: Jørn Utzon's design for the Opera House was chosen in January 1957 from 233 entries sent from 32 countries.

gives.name: Where to stand
gives.text: Light: a guide's sense of where the sun falls on the shells

request.text: Take one photograph at golden or blue hour (photo mode, O)
request.ask: The tiles go gold a little before sunset, then pink. Bring me one frame taken in that light.

ranks.title: The man who never saw it
talk: That's the light. You waited for it.
Utzon walked off the job in February 1966, over money and a minister. He left the country and never came back. Not once.
The Queen opened it in October 1973 without him. Here, I've set your camera the way the night photographers have theirs. See what the sails do after dark.
ranks.fact: Utzon resigned in February 1966 and never returned to Australia; Queen Elizabeth II opened the Opera House on 20 October 1973.

gives.name: Night sails
gives.text: Photographs after sunset come out on Marco's night film

request.text: Eat something by the water, as the audience does before a show
request.ask: Have you eaten? The counter at the Opera Bar is just along the concourse. Mind the gulls.

ranks.title: Ten thousand pipes
talk: Fed? Good. And the gulls had a look, I'm sure.
Inside the Concert Hall is the biggest mechanical organ in the world. More than ten thousand pipes. Ronald Sharp spent ten years building it and finished in 1979, six years after the doors opened.
ranks.fact: The Concert Hall's Grand Organ, completed by Ronald Sharp in 1979, has more than 10,000 pipes and is the largest mechanical-action organ in the world.

gives.name: A guide's eye
gives.text: Light, from someone who has watched these shells for years

request.text: See the sails from Mrs Macquarie's Chair, in the evening
request.ask: Walk round Farm Cove to Mrs Macquarie's Chair one evening. From there the shells and the bridge line up.

ranks.title: On the list
talk: You saw them line up. That's the postcard, and it's a fifteen-minute walk most visitors never take.
In 2007 this went on the World Heritage list. Utzon was eighty-nine and alive to hear it. He died the next year, and he never did see it finished.
I tell that story six times a day and it still gets me. Come on a tour some time. Stand at the back and heckle.
ranks.fact: The Sydney Opera House was added to the World Heritage List in 2007, in Jørn Utzon's lifetime; he died in 2008 without having seen it completed.

gives.name: Marco's word
gives.text: 20% more for every job in Sydney

bonds.title: The bridge climber
bonds.busy: Done for the day, and my legs know it. I'm here mornings and through the day, between climbs.

ranks.title: The pylons
ranks.invite: You came over on the ferry looking straight up, I saw you. Got a bit of the {slot}? I'll tell you the bridge's best secret.
talk: They built the arch as two halves, reaching out from each shore on cables. The halves touched on the nineteenth of August 1930, and the whole town stopped to look.
Now look at the four stone towers. Eighty-nine metres each, faced in granite shipped up from Moruya, down the south coast.
ranks.fact: The Harbour Bridge's four 89 m pylons, faced with granite from Moruya, carry none of the arch's load.

ask.q: What do you reckon they hold up?

options.reply: Nothing. The arch sits on four steel bearings down by the water. The pylons are there so people would trust it.
That's what you're meant to think. The arch sits on steel bearings by the water. The pylons carry nothing: they're there so people would trust it.

request.text: Take a ferry across the harbour
request.ask: Take a ferry and look up as you go. You'll see the bearings at the waterline, one pair each end of the arch.

ranks.title: Six million rivets
talk: See them? Everything above you rests on those four pins.
Six million rivets hold it together. Each one was heated on the steel, thrown, caught in a bucket and hammered home by hand. The last went in on 21 January 1932.
ranks.fact: About six million hand-driven rivets hold the Harbour Bridge together; the last was driven on 21 January 1932.

gives.name: A climber's bearings
gives.text: Bearings: you know the harbour from above

request.text: Walk up to the trig station at the middle of the arch
request.ask: Walk the deck to the middle of the arch. There's a trig station there. Come back and tell me which way the Heads are.

ranks.title: A warm day
talk: East, out past the Opera House. Good. Did you feel it move when a train went under you?
On a hot day the steel swells and the top of the arch lifts about eighteen centimetres. Before they opened it they parked ninety-six steam engines on it, end to end. It hardly noticed.
Kev fishes under the south end most mornings. He left his thermos on the first ferry and it's in my locker. Run it over to him? There's a few dollars in it from the crew's tin.
ranks.fact: On hot days the top of the Harbour Bridge's arch rises by about 18 cm; in February 1932 it was load-tested with as many as 96 steam locomotives.

gives.name: Lena's errand
gives.text: A paid delivery across the harbour, in your diary under Work

request.text: Take Kev's thermos to him, under the south end of the bridge
request.ask: The thermos is here when you're ready. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: The ribbon
talk: Kev says ta. He also says the bream were off, so don't expect a fish.
Opening day, 19 March 1932. The Premier's standing there with his scissors, and a bloke called de Groot rides up on a horse and cuts the ribbon with a sword.
They arrested him, tied the ribbon back together and did it again properly.
ranks.fact: On opening day, 19 March 1932, Francis de Groot rode up on horseback and slashed the ribbon with his sword before the Premier, Jack Lang, could cut it.

request.text: Guess a building's height to within a quarter (G)
request.ask: Fancy your eye? Pick a tower over the water, press G, and tell me how close you got.

ranks.title: First light
talk: That's a good eye for a height. You'd be right at home up there.
The public's only been allowed over the arch since 1998. Before that it belonged to the riggers and the painters. Paul Hogan was one of them, before the telly found him.
First light from the top, with the ferries just starting. If you ever want it, ask for me.
ranks.fact: Public climbs over the arch of the Harbour Bridge began in 1998; until then only riggers, painters and maintenance crews went up.

gives.name: The view from the top
gives.text: Bearings, from someone who works above the harbour

bonds.title: The barista at Barangaroo
bonds.where: Barangaroo Reserve, by the coffee cart
bonds.busy: Machine's off and I'm cleaning down. I pull shots mornings and through the day. Come back then.

ranks.title: Barangaroo
ranks.invite: You've walked the whole foreshore, haven't you? Sit. Got a bit of the {slot}? I'll tell you whose place this is.
talk: This headland's named for a woman. Barangaroo, a Cammeraygal fisher, here when the First Fleet came in. She thought very little of the newcomers and said so.
She was married to Bennelong. He got the point with the Opera House on it. She got this one, and I reckon hers is nicer.
ranks.fact: Barangaroo is named after a Cammeraygal woman of the 1790s, a fisher and the wife of Bennelong.

ask.q: The headland's all sandstone blocks. Where d'you reckon the stone came from?

options.reply: Right under where the car park is now. Ten thousand blocks, and nine in ten of them were cut on the spot.
Closer than that. They cut it out of the ground right here: ten thousand blocks, nine in ten from the site.

request.ask: Have you had a coffee yet today? The cart's right there. First one I'll make properly.

ranks.title: The Hungry Mile
talk: Sydney says it invented the flat white. So does Wellington. I stay out of it.
The road behind us is Hickson Road. In the Depression the wharfies called it the Hungry Mile. You walked it wharf to wharf every morning, hoping to be picked for a day's work.
I've an order going up to the Observatory every day, and my knees are done with that hill. Want it?
ranks.fact: In the Great Depression, wharf labourers called the Hickson Road waterfront the Hungry Mile, walking from wharf to wharf each day in search of work.

gives.name: Noor's hill run
gives.text: A paid coffee run up Observatory Hill, in your diary under Work

request.text: Carry the coffees up to Observatory Hill
request.ask: Tray's ready when you are. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: The old shoreline
talk: Still hot when they got there? Then you ran.
Until 2015 this was flat concrete with containers stacked on it. They built the headland back along the line of the 1836 shore, off old maps and paintings, and opened it that August.
ranks.fact: Barangaroo Reserve opened on 22 August 2015 on a former container wharf, its shoreline remade along the foreshore of 1836.

request.text: Climb to the trig station on top of Barangaroo Reserve
request.ask: Walk up to the top of the headland. There's a trig station on the crown, and the whole west harbour under it.

ranks.title: Kingfish
talk: Good view, isn't it. You can see every ferry coming.
The path along the water is Wulugul Walk. Wulugul is kingfish, in the Sydney language. They say the gold stripe down the fish is the sandstone along the water's edge.
ranks.fact: Wulugul Walk, the foreshore path at Barangaroo, is named with the Sydney-language word for kingfish.

gives.name: A barista's palate
gives.text: Taste: you know a good cup from a hot one

request.text: Stand under Crown Sydney after dark
request.ask: Walk down past the towers one night. The tall one with the twist in it: stand at the bottom and look straight up.

ranks.title: The tall one
talk: Makes your neck hurt, doesn't it.
Two hundred and seventy-one metres. Tallest building in Sydney since 2020. Sydney Tower goes higher, but that's a spire with a turret on it, not somewhere you'd rent a desk.
When I started the cart there was a crane where that is. Come by any morning. You're a regular now, and regulars don't queue.
ranks.fact: Crown Sydney at Barangaroo, finished in 2020 and 271 m tall, is the tallest building in Sydney; only Sydney Tower's spire stands higher.

gives.name: Regular's cup
gives.text: Taste, from someone who knows her customers

bonds.title: The Hyde Park regular
bonds.where: Hyde Park, by the Archibald Fountain
bonds.busy: Bench is wet, or it's not my hour. I'm here most dry days, from lunchtime till the lamps come on.

ranks.title: The family in the fountain
ranks.invite: You've walked a way. Sit down. Got a bit of the {slot}? I'll introduce you to the family in the fountain.
talk: That's Apollo on top with his arm out. Diana's below with her deer, and round the far side Theseus is sorting out the Minotaur.
A Frenchman made it in Paris, Sicard. Archibald, who ran the Bulletin, left the money and said it had to be a Frenchman. He got one.
ranks.fact: The Archibald Fountain in Hyde Park, unveiled in 1932, was made in Paris by François Sicard with a bequest from J. F. Archibald of the Bulletin.

ask.q: What was this park before it was a park, do you reckon?

options.reply: Racecourse, cricket pitch, parade ground. The first proper races in the colony were run round here in 1810. You know your parks.
No, the old burial ground's under Town Hall. This was the racecourse: the first proper races in the colony, 1810.

request.text: Guess a building's height to within a quarter (G)
request.ask: Go on, try your eye. Pick a tower, press G. Get inside a quarter and you've beaten me.

ranks.title: Stars in the dome
talk: Better than me. I'm always twenty metres out.
Down the south end, past the pool, is the Anzac Memorial. Look up inside: a hundred and twenty thousand gold stars in the dome, for the men and women from this state who went to the first war.
My grandfather's one of them. I couldn't tell you which.
ranks.fact: The dome of the Anzac Memorial in Hyde Park, opened in 1934, carries 120,000 gold stars for the people of New South Wales who served in the First World War.

request.text: Walk down to the Anzac Memorial, at the south end of Hyde Park
request.ask: Have you been down to the Memorial? South end, past the Pool of Reflection. Take your hat off inside.

ranks.title: Thirty years on the meter
talk: You went down. Good on you.
I drove a cab in this town for thirty years. Half the drivers on the ranks, I showed them the back way to the airport. Tell them Tom from the Park Street rank sent you.
Up the top end, the long brick building is the Barracks. A convict designed it for convicts: Greenway, 1819. It's World Heritage now. He'd have laughed.
ranks.fact: Hyde Park Barracks, designed by the convict architect Francis Greenway and finished in 1819, has been on the World Heritage List since 2010.

gives.name: Tom's old rank
gives.text: 25% off every taxi and ride in Sydney

request.ask: Have you had a pie yet? The cart's just along the path. Sauce on top, no arguments.

ranks.title: The big one

needs.text: Keep guessing heights a while. When your eye's in, I've a big one for you.

talk: Sauce on top? You'll do.
Now the big one. Sydney Tower, there over the trees: three hundred and nine metres to the tip. It opened in 1981 and nothing in this city has gone higher since.
The turret hangs in a net of fifty-six cables. I watched them string it from this bench.
ranks.fact: Sydney Tower, 309 m to the tip of its spire, opened to the public in 1981 and remains the tallest structure in Sydney.

request.text: Photograph Sydney Tower from the park (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Take us a picture of the tower from the park, would you? Photo mode. I'll tell you if it's straight.

ranks.title: The oldest park
talk: That's straight. Straighter than the tower looks, some days.
Macquarie named this Hyde Park in 1810, and it's been common ground ever since. Oldest public park in the country. They only finished the spires on St Mary's in 2000, mind.
Come and sit any dry afternoon. I'll keep you the end with the shade.
ranks.fact: Hyde Park, about 16 hectares in the middle of Sydney and named by Governor Macquarie in 1810, is the oldest public parkland in Australia.

gives.name: Tom's eye
gives.text: Eye, from thirty years of judging a fare by the look of it

jobs.title: Coffees for Observatory Hill
jobs.blurb: Four flat whites from Noor's cart at Barangaroo up to the top of Observatory Hill, before they go cold.
jobs.text: Four flat whites in a cardboard tray. Up the steps, not round by the road.
jobs.done: The astronomers look up, for once.

jobs.title: Which way from the Quay?
jobs.blurb: Visitors off the ferries ask the way. Face each place's true bearing; the nearer, the better the pay.
jobs.who: A couple off a cruise ship
jobs.done: They set off the right way, arguing about lunch.

jobs.title: Three for the postcard rack
jobs.blurb: A kiosk on the Quay wants new postcards: the Opera House, the Harbour Bridge and Customs House. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: The kiosk prints fifty of each.

jobs.title: A fare to Hyde Park
jobs.blurb: Drive your own car as a cab: pick up beside Customs House and take your passenger up through the city to Park Street, in Hyde Park.
jobs.who: A woman with a cello case
jobs.text: "Park Street, by the fountain. I'm playing a wedding at one and the cello doesn't run."

jobs.title: Kev's thermos
jobs.blurb: From Milsons Point to the seawall under the south end of the bridge: over the water by ferry and round through the Rocks, or across the bridge on foot.
jobs.to_name: Kev, under the south end of the bridge
jobs.text: One dented steel thermos, still warm. He'll be on the seawall at Dawes Point with a line in.
jobs.done: Kev pours you the first cup.

shops.name: Quay kiosk
shops.where: Circular Quay, by the ferry wharves
shops.hello: G'day. Drinks are cold, ferries are that way.

menu.name: Lemon, lime and bitters
menu.text: Lemonade, lime cordial and a few dashes of bitters over ice, pink at the top. Every pub and kiosk in Australia will make you one.

menu.name: A tin ferry
menu.text: A small tin harbour ferry in green and cream, with a bow at both ends so it never has to turn round.

shops.name: Noor's coffee cart
shops.hello: Morning. What can I get you?

menu.name: Flat white
menu.text: A double shot under a thin layer of steamed milk, no froth to speak of. Sydney cafes were pouring them by the mid-1980s; Wellington claims it too.

menu.name: Banana bread, toasted
menu.text: A thick slice, toasted, with butter going into it. It is in the cabinet of nearly every cafe in Sydney.

shops.name: Opera Bar counter
shops.where: The Lower Concourse, under the Opera House
shops.hello: Order here, find a spot on the wall. Watch the gulls.

menu.name: Hot chips
menu.text: A box of hot chips with chicken salt, eaten on the seawall with one hand over the top. The silver gulls know exactly how long you will last.

menu.name: Sydney rock oysters, half a dozen
menu.text: Small, sweet and mineral, with a wedge of lemon. Sydney rock oysters are native to this coast and take about three years to grow.

shops.name: Pie cart
shops.where: Hyde Park, near the Archibald Fountain
shops.hello: Pies are hot. Sauce is on the side of the cart.

menu.name: Meat pie with sauce
menu.text: Minced beef and gravy in a hand-sized pastry case, tomato sauce squeezed on the lid. You eat it from the paper bag, and it is hotter than it looks.

menu.name: Lamington
menu.text: A square of sponge dipped in chocolate icing and rolled in coconut. Named for Lord Lamington, Governor of Queensland around 1900.

events.title: Vivid Sydney
events.text: Three weeks of light on the harbour's buildings each winter, from late May to mid-June: 28 May to 19 June in 2027.
lines: At dusk the sails stop being white. Colour runs up them from the podium, and the forecourt goes quiet for a second before every phone comes out.
Vivid began in 2009, when Brian Eno lit these shells. It has run in late May and June in most years since, right round the Quay.

events.title: New Year's Eve on the harbour
events.verb: Find a patch of grass and wait for midnight
events.text: Fireworks over the harbour at 9pm and again at midnight, with the Harbour Bridge in the middle of them.
lines: Picnic rugs, edge to edge. Nobody gives up a spot here: at most of the harbour's vantage points, if you leave you do not get back in.
At nine the first fireworks go up. At midnight the bridge itself goes off, the whole arch at once, and the harbour answers.

events.title: Australia Day Ferrython
events.text: On 26 January, a little after midday, four Sydney ferries race across the harbour to a finish off the Opera House.
lines: Four Emerald-class ferries dressed in flags, every passenger at the rail. The start is at about ten past twelve.
They were not built to race. They do it anyway, bow to bow, to a finish line off the Opera House, and the whole foreshore picks a boat to yell for.

events.title: Anzac Day dawn service
events.verb: Stand with the crowd in the dark
events.text: Each 25 April, before first light, thousands stand in Martin Place for the dawn service at the Cenotaph.
lines: A little after four, and Martin Place is full and silent. The only light is on the Cenotaph: a soldier and a sailor in bronze, either end of a block of granite.
The Last Post, a minute's silence, then Reveille as the sky greys over Macquarie Street. Later in the morning the march goes down Elizabeth Street.

events.title: Jacaranda season
events.text: From mid-October the jacarandas round Circular Quay and the Rocks flower purple, and by November they are full.
lines: The trees flower before they leaf, so for a few weeks there is nothing overhead but purple, and the path under them turns the same colour.
They came from South America. Sydney students say that if the jacarandas are out and you have not started studying, it is already too late.
